newsitem.title: USA: EMI buys half of classic Motown song catalog.
newsitem.headline: EMI buys half of classic Motown song catalog.

text.p: In what it described as one of the biggest deals in music publishing history, EMI Group said on Tuesday it paid $132 million for a 50 percent share in the company that controls the classic Motown songs.
The sale covers the copyrights to timeless tunes performed by the likes of the Temptations, Stevie Wonder, Smokey Robinson and the Miracles, Marvin Gaye, Jackie Wilson and the Jackson 5.

The songs were owned by Berry Gordy Jr., the one-time Detroit autoworker who founded Motown Records in 1959 and went on to shape rock 'n' roll history. He sold the label to PolyGram NV in 1991 for $301 million, but held on to the crown jewel of his empire, the Jobete Music publishing companies.

Music publishing is regarded as a license to print money, since songs generate income for the copyright holder each time they are played on the radio, covered by another artist or featured in a movie or advertisement. Many songwriters sell their publishing rights, but they still collect a "mechanical royalty" of about 3.3 cents per song whenever the songs are sold on an album or single.

In Jobete's case, the 15,000-strong catalog earned profits of about $10 million on gross revenues of about $25 million in the last full year, said Martin Bandier, chairman of New York-based EMI Music Publishing.

Rarely minutes go by when Motown songs such as Gaye's "I Heard it through the Grapevine," the Miracles' "Shop Around" or Barrett Strong's "Money" aren't being played in some incarnation in some part of the world.

"These songs represent the driving force in American and international music for the '60s, '70s and '80s," Bandier said in an interview. "Berry is a songwriter and an entrepreneur who put together the most spectacular group of songs that anyone could think of in the 20th Century."

Gordy, who turns 68 at the end of November, approached EMI a year ago about a possible deal, Bandier said. EMI, the world's largest music publisher with a catalog of just over a million songs, has administered the Motown catalog overseas for the past dozen years.
"For him, it was not necessarily about the money, but more about the structure of the deal and who is going to take care of the songs, because each one of them is like his children," Bandier said.

Indeed, Jobete takes its name from Gordy's first three children, JOy, BErry -- who ran Jobete's day-to-day operations - - and TErry. Additionally, Gordy co-wrote many of the songs, such as Wilson's "Reet Petite," the Contours' "Do You Love Me," and the Jackson 5's "I'll Be There" and "ABC"

EMI has first right of refusal on the rest of Jobete, which the parties expect will be worth considerably more than the first half. In the meantime, Jobete's staff of 35 to 40 people will lose their jobs when EMI closes Jobete's Los Angeles office and shifts its operations to New York, Bandier said.

Bandier said Gordy would serve as a "major consultant" to Jobete and focus on Motown-related activities, such as developing a stage play called "Do You Love Me," and several feature film and television projects.
EMI aims to expand Jobete's revenue base by aggressive marketing and promotion, both to the film and advertising communities and to new media areas such as karaoke, DVD and CD-ROM.
"Much of this has not been done in the recent past by Jobete," Bandier said. "That's stuff that we're great at."
Additionally, EMI has much muscle overseas and has just opened offices in Poland, Hungary, Croatia and the Czech Republic.

The last high-profile music publishing deal was in November 1995 when Michael Jackson merged his ATV Songs company, which owns many of the Beatles' copyrights, with Sony Music's publishing arm in a deal that gave him half of the combined entity and a reported payout of at least $110 million.
